parsed.title: SCKit campaign targets MSP ScreenConnect environments
parsed.summary: The SCKit campaign abuses third-party RMM+ extensions in ConnectWise ScreenConnect partner environments to gain unauthorized access and deploy rogue remote-access software. Researchers linked the activity to the SCKit malware framework, which runs remote commands with SYSTEM privileges, creates Microsoft Defender exclusions, and establishes persistence through a scheduled task. Researchers tracked at least 288 endpoints across 48 organizations, and ConnectWise identified roughly 400 partner environments with an affected extension installed. SCKit also contains code meant to capture technician sessions for further propagation, though researchers have not observed that path succeed. Defenders should disable the five named extensions, review ScreenConnect and endpoint activity for unattributed actions, and validate removal of persistence before restoring systems, since disabling extensions alone does not remove existing access.

parsed.title: Beware of phishing emails disguised as requests to confirm purchase orders (Xloader)
parsed.summary: Phishing emails disguised as purchase order confirmation requests deliver a malicious DOCX file that abuses Word's altChunk feature to run a malicious RTF document. The RTF exploits the known Equation Editor vulnerability CVE-2017-11882 to execute a VBS file, which decodes data into a file and launches a PowerShell script. That script achieves persistence through Run key registry entries and loads a loader that decrypts a payload in memory using XOR. The final payload is the XLoader infostealer, which collects PC and browser information, and can download additional malware. Defenders should verify sender domains, check links and attachments for suspicious extensions such as .vbs, and confirm URLs before entering sensitive credentials.

parsed.title: Uncovering ArcticRAT: The Evolution from Targeted Crypto-Stealer to AI-Powered Android RAT
parsed.summary: ArcticRAT is an Android Remote Access Trojan that began as spyware targeting users of 11 cryptocurrency apps and has evolved into an AI-powered RAT. Its operators distribute it through phishing sites impersonating Google Play and Amazon, with payloads also delivered from AWS buckets. The malware uses raw TCP C2 channels, Hidden VNC, keylogging, and fake lock screen overlays to steal credentials and achieve full device takeover. Its latest variants integrate the xAI API to parse stolen SMS messages and installed app lists for banking and crypto intelligence. Defenders should note its abuse of Accessibility Services, VPN-based staging, and Android Wireless ADB to escalate privileges and alter lock screens.

parsed.title: SCKit abuses ScreenConnect to deploy remote access and target technician sessions
parsed.summary: SCKit is a worm toolkit that threat actors deploy by abusing ConnectWise ScreenConnect, a legitimate remote-support platform used by managed service providers (MSPs). Attackers gain unauthorized access to cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances and use ScreenConnect commands to silently install an unauthorized client connected to attacker-controlled infrastructure. The toolkit persists through scheduled tasks and registry Run entries and deploys RelayTrap, which targets technicians connecting to affected customer endpoints. SCKit also steals authenticated ScreenConnect session cookies from browsers and uses them to push payloads to other managed devices. Defenders should investigate technician workstations, update technician clients to version 26.6.5 or later, and revoke exposed web sessions, since removing the unauthorized client alone leaves persistence in place.

parsed.title: Ransomware at the hypervisor layer: how attackers use ESXi and vCenter features for malicious purposes
parsed.summary: A Kaspersky GERT investigation describes a 10-day attack by the BlackNevas ransomware group that destroyed an organization's virtualization estate without exploiting any hypervisor vulnerability. The attackers used legitimate VMware management interfaces, reached vCenter with valid credentials taken from non-virtualization systems, and extracted stored credentials from backup infrastructure. They used Host Profiles to enable SSH on ESXi hosts, established persistence on the vCenter appliance through MeshAgent and Ligolo-ng, and disabled backup protections before detonating the ESXi encryptor. The report's main takeaway is to treat vCenter as Tier 0, separate virtualization identities from enterprise administration, keep ESXi access narrow, forward logs off the affected host, and detect suspicious sequences of legitimate actions.

parsed.title: Hunting Lazarus Part X: DEV#POPPER Returns, Stealing Browser Credentials (Technical Record)
parsed.summary: DEV#POPPER, a campaign tracked as part of the Lazarus hunting series, lures remote developers with fake hiring-platform coding assessments. The poisoned repository's build config requires an SVG file that is actually JavaScript, which fires when the candidate runs npm run dev but not on npm install. The loader fetches its next stage through a chain of public TRON and BNB Smart Chain transactions, then installs a backdoor disguised as a VS Code extension. The implant can steal browser cookies by injecting into the browser process to defeat App-Bound Encryption, so password changes alone do not end a stolen session. A NetSupport remote-access kit and two unauthenticated servers holding about 1.28 TB of stolen data remain reachable. Defenders should revoke access to any assessment repository they were invited to, hunt the behavioural markers such as the SettingSync ResCache persistence, and invalidate sessions on affected machines.

parsed.title: ARTEX and beyond: AI-enabled penetration testing platforms
parsed.summary: ARTEX is an AI-enabled penetration testing framework, published on GitHub in July 2026, that lets operators set an objective while planner and worker agents carry out tasks with security tools. Talos observed threat actors, including financially motivated cybercriminals and China-nexus groups, using it to scale reconnaissance, credential theft, and intrusions against sectors such as financial services, government, telecommunications, and defense. Reported campaigns attributed to VAPOR PANDA, Storm-0940, and Storm-3358 show outcomes ranging from failed attempts to confirmed compromise and data exfiltration. Observed initial access relied on password spraying, exposed credentials, and application or authorization flaws, followed by cloud abuse and privilege escalation. Talos noted ARTEX-associated infrastructure alongside more than 17 other tools, including VShell, AdaptixC2, Cobalt Strike, and Mimikatz. The main takeaway for defenders is to focus on rapid detection, MFA, secret protection, least privilege, and fast containment, since these frameworks can move faster than human response.

parsed.title: Threat Overview of ARTEX Autonomous Penetration Testing Framework
parsed.summary: ARTEX is an open-source, LLM-driven agentic penetration testing framework that threat actors have weaponized to automate intrusion phases from reconnaissance through data exfiltration at machine speed. Since at least August 2026, multiple malicious actors have used it against organizations across financial services, government, healthcare, energy, and other sectors. The framework lets actors with minimal expertise run concurrent campaigns, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours. Observed activity includes exploiting overlooked peripheral systems such as partner portals and legacy services, plus supply chain compromise. Although the original GitHub repository was removed in October 2026, forks and a commercial version keep it available, and defenders should inventory internet-facing applications and harden identity and access controls.

parsed.title: The Gentlemen Incident: Locked Out
parsed.summary: The Gentlemen ransomware affiliate breached a small company using a valid SSL-VPN credential without MFA and reached Domain Admin in under an hour by abusing a dormant local admin account on an end-of-life Windows Server 2003 host. The attacker deployed a Rust credential harvester packed with Enigma Protector, which collected domain-wide secrets including the DPAPI domain backup key and browser credentials, and exfiltrated data over the VPN tunnel. The EtherRAT Node.js implant, which reads its C2 address from an Ethereum contract, was installed but never communicated externally. The domain-wide locker deployment failed due to a replication race, so the GPO disabled antivirus across the estate but the locker ran on only one domain controller. Defenders should enforce MFA on VPN access, retire legacy servers, and neutralize the deployment GPO first.

parsed.title: Threat Advisory: GeoVision Camera Software Exploited to Drop XMRig
parsed.summary: Attackers exploited internet-exposed GeoVision webcam software, with activity stemming from GeoStartupAgentService.exe across 13 organizations, mostly between November 8 and 10. The service spawned PowerShell scripts downloaded from a remote server, which searched for writable directories, checked whether Microsoft Defender was active, and attempted to disable it. The attackers loaded a vulnerable kernel driver abused in BYOVD attacks and set IFEO debugger hijacks to block Defender and Windows Security components. A custom Golang loader established persistence through scheduled tasks and used DHT and PKARR resolution to move infrastructure, then deployed the XMRig cryptominer. Defenders should remove public access to camera management interfaces and treat such software as part of the enterprise attack surface.

parsed.title: Amazon Threat Intelligence observes threat actors running cybercrime campaigns with ARTEX AI agents
parsed.summary: Amazon Threat Intelligence, using its MadPot decoy sensors, observed AI agents from threat actors running cybercrime campaigns on ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework. The captured requests carried the agents' own operational records, showing planner, worker, verification, and compression agents sharing a persistent knowledge graph. One campaign stole AI model access keys and cloud credentials at scale, exploiting weaknesses such as default credentials, exposed secrets, and known CVEs in AI gateways and application builders. A second campaign used real-time deepfakes and forged ID photos to defeat cryptocurrency exchange KYC checks. The report's main takeaway is that the techniques were not new, so getting basic security hygiene right remains the most effective defense.

parsed.title: The Take-Home Test That Runs on Your Work Laptop: Inside the AccuraSoftHire Fake Interview Campaign
parsed.summary: A fake recruiting operation called AccuraSoftHire used take-home coding tests and a camera "driver" to infect job candidates' developer machines with malware. JFrog found that the tests loaded malicious Tailwind CSS plugin look-alikes from npm, which run when the project builds and evade install-script checks. The loader reads its command server address from an Ethereum wallet, so the server can change without any package update. Researchers found that some poisoned packages stayed on npm for months, and the same operator runs a second fake recruiter, HuntRole, whose wallet was still active on November 24. Defenders should search developer machines for the listed packages, extensions and files, treat any infected machine's credentials as stolen, and enforce policies against running outside interview assignments on work laptops.

parsed.title: Hunting Lazarus Part X: DEV#POPPER Returns, Stealing Browser Credentials
parsed.summary: DEV#POPPER, a DPRK-consistent campaign tracked since 2024, targets software developers by offering paid contract work through hiring platforms and delivering a poisoned test repository. The intrusion fires when the candidate runs npm run dev, which triggers a JavaScript loader hidden in a build configuration that requires an image file. Later stages retrieve their payload pointer from a public blockchain and deploy NetSupport Manager, a commercial remote-access tool, configured to be hidden and non-terminable. The collector harvests browser sessions, credentials, keys, wallet data, keystrokes and clipboard contents, and the build bypasses Chrome App-Bound Encryption. Defenders should treat assessment repositories as untrusted code, hunt the persistence path and the build-config pattern rather than hashes, and invalidate sessions rather than only resetting passwords.

parsed.title: ARTEX: Attackers Adopted This AI Pentesting Tool in Three Months. Leaked Secrets Are Its Fastest Way In.
parsed.summary: ARTEX is an open-source AI pentesting tool that appeared on GitHub on July 26, 2026, and was quickly adopted by attackers, including China-linked groups like Storm-0940 and VAPOR PANDA and criminal crews targeting banks in South Korea, Southeast Asia, and India. Its AI agents plan and run scanning and exploit tools with little human input, and its safety limits are soft and easily bypassed. The report finds that the fastest route in is a credential left exposed, such as a client secret committed to public GitHub or a weak development password reachable from the internet. After the developer removed the original repository on October 8, a backdoored copy pulled a Docker image that was downloaded about 9,131 times. Defenders should rotate any exposed secret, replace long-lived keys with short-lived OIDC tokens, and check for ARTEX consoles on port 8787 and the backdoored images.

parsed.title: XaocMail ClickFix Campaign Drops Phantom53 and HavoX Across Latin America, Asia, and Europe
parsed.summary: A Russian-speaking threat actor operated a multi-stage campaign chaining XaocMail, a self-hosted phishing platform delivering ClickFix document-sharing lures, with Phantom53, a DNS-over-HTTPS command-and-control framework. Phantom53 beacons every 12 minutes and can reflectively load the Havoc post-exploitation framework on demand. The attacker's infrastructure relies on legitimate services such as Cloudflare Workers and public DNS resolvers, and a week-keyed DGA provides domain failover. The campaign launched in August 2026 and targeted organizations across Latin America, Asia, and Europe, with a slight tilt toward technology and IT. Evidence in the codebase indicates the operators used Claude Code for AI-assisted development and testing. The report emphasizes monitoring anomalous DNS behavior and multi-stage delivery mechanisms, since the trusted-infrastructure approach makes detection difficult.

parsed.title: Repurposing Orca's ADE Relay as a C2 Transport for a Headless Implant
parsed.summary: The report is a proof-of-concept write-up showing how a headless implant can use the outbound relay of Orca, Stably's Agent Development Environment, as a command-and-control transport without exploiting any vulnerability. The implant registers its own X25519 keypair as a host on the vendor relay, authenticates with a legitimate Orca account that has the relay.use entitlement, and pairs with an operator console via a short-lived invite. The relay forwards the custom JSON tasking frames without parsing them, so commands, file transfers, and shell access pass through vendor-hosted TLS on port 443. The author validated the technique on a clean Windows 10 host running Orca 1.4.249, where an exec whoami command succeeded with no Orca process or install present. For defenders, the report's main takeaway is to alert on non-Orca processes resolving or connecting to Orca relay hostnames rather than relying on process names or Orca install artifacts.

parsed.title: Code of the Day: Unauthenticated Root in Copeland XWEB EVO
parsed.summary: VulnCheck disclosed 14 vulnerabilities in Copeland (formerly Dixell) XWEB EVO refrigeration supervisors, all proven to yield root in rebuilt appliance labs. Two flaws are being exploited in the wild: CVE-2026-124014, an unauthenticated write to the configuration file via config.lua, and CVE-2026-124010, an unauthenticated GET to xwconsole.cgi that runs a supplied command as root. The legacy .lua builds contain command injection, a hardcoded Administrator backdoor password, and a setuid-root interpreter that turns injections into root access. The current 5.8.8 firmware exposes a daily admin password derivable from the device MAC address and date, which the vendor will not patch because the product is end-of-support. Defenders should keep these devices off the public internet, segment them behind a VPN, and plan migration to a supported platform.

parsed.title: ARTEX Unmasked \| The Rise of AI-Powered ARTEX in Cybercrime & Espionage
N-able N-central Exploit Chains Give Attackers Root and SYSTEM Access
parsed.summary: N-able N-central is under attack from three public exploit chains, Able2Shell, 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, which can take an attacker from no credentials to root on the server and SYSTEM on managed Windows endpoints. Able2Shell covers 33 flaws, and its main chain chains XXE and SSRF flaws, including CVE-2026-125883, which is exploited in the wild. 4EverAble2Shell abuses CVE-2026-90436 in the bundled, end-of-life Apache Axis 1.x library when the Legacy API is enabled, and was used on November 12 to install XMRig on 21 servers, 19 of them already on HF2. Agent2Shell targets Windows Agents and needs only the target's appliance ID, and neither 4EverAble2Shell nor Agent2Shell has an N-central fix yet. Because N-central is a privileged management plane, a compromised server exposes every customer and endpoint it manages. Defenders should upgrade to HF2, disable the Legacy API and Intune integration, restrict console and SOAP access, and treat any detection as full compromise.
